newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany slams blanket indictment of Hitler's army.
newsitem.headline: Germany slams blanket indictment of Hitler's army.

text.p: German politicians, reacting to a controversial exhibition on the wartime crimes of Hitler's Wehrmacht army, spoke out on Thursday against blanket indictments of its role in the Holocaust and other Nazi horrors.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition said it did not want the German parliament to host the hard-hitting photo exhibition showing Wehrmacht troops killing Jews in the Soviet Union and partisans in Yugoslavia.

The exhibition, which prompted neo-Nazi protests when it opened in Munich last month, shatters the post-war myth of a "clean" Wehrmacht that stood apart from the SS troops said to have carried out massacres of Jews on the eastern front.

But parliament postponed a vote on a government motion which "firmly rejects any one-sided or blanket indictment of members of the Wehrmacht", worded to please conservatives outraged by the exhibition's attack on the Wehrmacht's honour.

The parliament hosted an emotional debate during which some deputies broke down crying at the speaker's podium as they told harrowing tales of their families' sufferings and gave embarrassing details of rabid Nazis among their relatives.
"Even 52 years after the end of World War Two, it is still not easy to speak about the role of the Wehrmacht," Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said.

He said the Wehrmacht had served the Nazi dictatorship but pointed out there were also officers who had revolted and tried to assassinate Hitler in 1944. Many soldiers thought they were fighting for their fatherland, only to be misused by the Nazis.

"The experiences of the Wehrmacht soldier are the experiences of our father's generation. Its effects are still felt in many families. It is our responsibilty to approach our past critically," Ruehe said.
"It is too simplistic to speak about "the' Wehrmacht...this way of speaking leads to false assignments of guilt," he said.

Meanwhile, the upper house of parliament presented a resolution to pardon all Wehrmacht deserters and those who had been convicted of avoiding military service during the war and offer them some financial compensation.
The federal office for victims of the Nazi justice system said about 200 men would be affected by the law.
